questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [mid] multi-tenant isolation for a B2B CRUD app (grok-build-multitenant, dfableandopus/05-SYSTEM-DESIGN-FOLLOWUPS.md). Scenario: a projects-and-tasks SaaS serves 2,000 customer organizations today and plans for 10,000; the largest tenant holds 400,000 projects; a user can belong to several organizations and picks one per request; three API instances sit behind a load balancer; members of one organization edit the same project at the same time. Write your design before you look: the tenancy model, where the tenant id is resolved and where it is enforced (request, service, repository, schema), how writes stay tenant-safe and conflict-safe, and how list reads stay predictable as tenants grow. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] One shared schema: every tenant-owned table carries the organization id and its indexes lead with it, so a query inside one tenant is an index range scan and adding tenants costs storage rather than query time.
keyPoints.quote: so a large tenant count costs storage, not query time

keyPoints.text: [w3] Enforcement is layered, not delegated: the request layer resolves which organization the caller may act in, the service checks the capability, and the repository still puts the organization id into every query predicate, because a correct membership check cannot repair an unscoped query.
keyPoints.quote: every where carries organizationId

keyPoints.text: [w3] Put the tenant rule in the schema where you can: a composite key (id, organization) on the parent and a child foreign key that carries the organization id make cross-tenant references structurally impossible, whichever service writes next.
keyPoints.quote: works the same at any scale

keyPoints.text: [w3] Concurrent edits use a conditional write: update where id, organization and expected version all match, bump the version, and require exactly one changed row; the database evaluates the predicate, so three instances race exactly like one.
[w2] Each mutation and its audit row commit in one transaction, so an accepted change and its audit trail can never disagree after a failure.
keyPoints.quote: keeps the current property that an effect and its record commit together

keyPoints.text: [w2] List reads are bounded: a fixed page size on the organization-leading index and a capped page number, with a cursor on the complete ordering tuple planned for when deep pages get expensive.
keyPoints.quote: The per-tenant read does, because the index leads with

keyPoints.text: [w2] Search needs its own index: a case-insensitive substring match cannot use a b-tree, so at scale it needs a trigram index, which is a migration and not a code change.
keyPoints.quote: cannot use a b-tree, so at a million rows it needs a

keyPoints.text: [w2] Creates get a client-generated key scoped to user, organization and operation, stored with a fingerprint of the validated payload and committed with the record and its audit, so a retried create returns the original id.
keyPoints.quote: scoped to the authenticated user, the organization and the operation

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the same app at 10x: 10,000 tenants, the biggest one at a million projects with users paging deep into the list, a new reporting query that forgets the organization predicate, and a credential-stuffing run against sign-in spread across the three instances. What breaks first, and what in your design already handles it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The forgotten predicate is a cross-tenant leak under convention-only isolation; row-level security keyed on a per-transaction tenant setting makes the same mistake return nothing instead.
keyPoints.quote: A forgotten predicate then returns nothing instead of returning someone else's rows

keyPoints.text: [w3] Offset paging breaks first for the biggest tenant: deep pages make the database walk and throw away rows, and the exact count rescans that tenant's filtered set on every request; a page cap only limits the damage.
keyPoints.quote: deep pages make PostgreSQL walk and discard rows

keyPoints.text: [w3] A login limiter held in process memory gives an attacker one budget per instance, so three instances triple the attempts; the limiter must move to shared state before scaling out.
keyPoints.quote: so three instances mean three times the attempt budget

keyPoints.text: [w2] The per-request membership lookup multiplies with instances and invites a cache; once cached, its TTL is how long a removed member keeps access, so the number is a written policy decision.
keyPoints.quote: the TTL becomes the revocation delay

keyPoints.text: [w2] Row-level security has its own failure mode: with connection pooling the tenant setting must be applied per transaction, or a pooled connection carries the previous request's tenant; table owners bypass policies unless they are forced.
keyPoints.quote: or a pooled connection carries the previous request's tenant

keyPoints.text: [w2] Side effects outside the database cannot be rolled back by it, so notifications go through an outbox row written in the same transaction and a separate worker; delivery is at-least-once.
keyPoints.quote: cannot roll back an email

keyPoints.text: [w1] The first alert to wire up is tenant-context refusals counted apart from capability refusals: the former is someone acting in an organization they do not belong to.
keyPoints.quote: which in a multi-tenant system is the alert you actually want

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your tenancy choices against the alternatives the doc names: shared schema versus schema per tenant versus database per tenant, predicates plus tests versus row-level security, offset versus keyset pagination, an advisory lock versus a unique index for idempotent creates, an outbox versus sending from the handler, and where the organization id goes in observability. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Shared schema keeps one migration and shared connection pools; schema per tenant buys hard isolation and per-tenant restore at the price of ten thousand migration copies and unshareable pools; database per tenant ends noisy neighbours but makes cross-tenant reporting painful.
keyPoints.quote: ten thousand copies of every migration

keyPoints.text: [w3] Row-level security converts a leak into an empty result, but it costs a raw per-transaction setting because the ORM has no first-class support, plus forced policies so owners cannot bypass them; without it the guarantee is convention plus an integration suite.
keyPoints.quote: Prisma has no first-class support, so it needs a raw

keyPoints.text: [w3] Keyset pagination on the ordering tuple keeps deep pages cheap but gives up jumping to an arbitrary page and an exact total.
keyPoints.quote: what is lost is jumping to page 40 and knowing the exact total

keyPoints.text: [w2] For idempotent creates the unique index on the receipt is what makes it correct; a per-caller lock only lets a concurrent duplicate come back as the original record instead of a constraint violation.
keyPoints.quote: The lock is not what makes it correct, the unique index is

keyPoints.text: [w2] An outbox keeps intent and record atomic and moves the unreliable send out of the request; its remaining crash window is closed by a receiver-honoured dedupe key, not a longer transaction.
keyPoints.quote: the mitigation is a deduplication key the receiver honours, not a longer transaction

keyPoints.text: [w1] The organization id belongs on every structured log line for per-tenant debugging, but not in metric labels, where it makes retention expensive.
keyPoints.quote: so it belongs in structured logs rather than in metric labels
